patient_information: A 3-year-old rural Lao boy who is up to date with vaccinations. His parents are rice farmers. The child is developing normally and has no known history of trauma. He has no previous ear infection or dental problems.
chief_complaint: 10-day history of gradual, painful swelling of the right cheek with associated fever and poor appetite.
history_of_present_illness: The boy presented with a 10-day history of gradual, painful swelling of the right cheek, accompanied by fever and poor appetite. Three days prior to presentation, his mother noticed a purulent discharge from the ear. He reported no cough, vomiting, or diarrhoea.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a rural Lao boy from a rice farming family and was likely frequently exposed to soil and water containing B. pseudomallei in the paddy fields. Melioidosis is endemic in Laos, where B. pseudomallei is readily isolated from soil and surface water, with most cases presenting during the rainy season.
physical_exam: The child appeared unwell. There was a localized, fluctuant, hot, tender swelling below and anterior to the right ear, measuring 6 to 8 cm in diameter, extending from the lower cheek to the submandibular region, consistent with a parotid mass. Ear examination revealed a purulent discharge in the auditory canal, suspicion of a small fistula from which the pus was arising, and a right lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy. The oral cavity and throat were unremarkable. There was no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, normal heart sounds, and a clear chest.
labs_and_diagnostics: Laboratory results showed a WBC of 16.5 ×10^9/L (normal range: 4–10 x10^9/L), with 90% neutrophils. Hemoglobin was 9.4g/dL (normal range: 13-15g/dL). All other blood tests were normal. Later, pus culture from the right ear and parotid abscess isolated B. pseudomallei. Blood culture was negative. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound were normal.
differential_diagnosis: Acute, suppurative, unilateral parotitis in children is usually bacterial, with common pathogens including Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Haemophilus influenzae. In endemic areas like Laos, Burkholderia pseudomallei, the causative agent of melioidosis, must also be considered, as studies in neighboring countries have shown it to be the commonest cause of suppurative parotitis in children. Less common bacterial causes include Actinomycosis and cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae). Mumps was considered but typically presents as non-suppurative and bilateral swelling. Other viral agents like parainfluenza, influenza A, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and enteroviruses were less likely due to the degree of inflammation and suppuration. Granulomatous parotitis caused by mycobacteria is rare and presents as a chronic, painless mass without inflammation. Salivary stones and malignancies are very rare in children.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient underwent incision and drainage of the parotid, which involved the removal of copious pus. Intravenous ceftazidime was administered for 10 days, followed by oral co-amoxiclav for 16 weeks. The patient showed a good clinical response, with no complications occurring and no underlying disease identified.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was melioidosis, caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. This was confirmed by pus culture from the right ear and parotid abscess, which isolated B. pseudomallei. Epidemiological factors, including the patient being from a rural Lao rice farming family with likely exposure to contaminated soil and water, supported the diagnosis. The patient responded well to incision and drainage followed by a course of intravenous ceftazidime and oral co-amoxiclav.
